title: Feeding the Axon: Glia as Metabolic Partners

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Which glia make myelin in the CNS, and which make it in peripheral nerves?
cards.back: Oligodendrocytes in the CNS; Schwann cells in peripheral nerves.
cards.quote: Myelinating glia, most clearly oligodendrocytes, which myelinate axons in the brain and spinal cord.

cards.front: Why does glial metabolic support not mean that an axon depends exclusively on glia for fuel?
cards.back: Axons also take up glucose directly and have their own mitochondria. Glial fuel supplements these sources.
cards.quote: Help, not sole supply. Axons still take up glucose and still have their own mitochondria.

cards.front: What does one ATP pay for in a cycle of the neuronal sodium-potassium pump?
cards.back: Moving three sodium ions out of the neuron and two potassium ions in.
cards.quote: spending one ATP to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in.
cards.section: An axon has a supply problem

cards.front: Why must a long axon make ATP locally rather than rely on ATP diffusing from its soma?
cards.back: Diffusion time grows with distance squared, and ATP is consumed along the way. Axonal mitochondria and glycolysis must supply ATP locally.
cards.quote: An axon's ATP has to be made locally, by axonal mitochondria and axonal glycolysis.
cards.section: An axon has a supply problem

cards.front: For ATP diffusing 1 millimetre along an axon, estimate the time using t ≈ L²/(2D) and D ≈ 150–300 µm²/s. Ignore ATP consumption.
cards.back: L = 1,000 µm. At D = 300, t ≈ 1,667 s ≈ 28 min; at D = 150, t ≈ 3,333 s ≈ 56 min. Thus about 28–56 min.
cards.quote: These rough estimates use time ≈ L²/2D, with a diffusion coefficient D for ATP in cytoplasm of about 150 to 300 µm² per second.
cards.section: An axon has a supply problem

cards.front: The short gaps where a myelinated axon's membrane is bare are the {{c1::nodes of Ranvier}}.
cards.quote: the nodes of Ranvier, the short gaps where the axon membrane is bare.
cards.section: An axon has a supply problem

cards.front: Why does extensive myelin coverage make glial fuel delivery plausible without proving it is necessary?
cards.back: Myelin limits direct access to extracellular glucose, but glucose entering at nodes and under myelin might suffice. Geometry alone cannot establish a need for glial fuel.
cards.quote: So the geometry makes glial supply plausible; it does not prove the axon needs it.
cards.section: An axon has a supply problem

cards.front: Model a continuously myelinated CNS axon as repeating units with a 50 µm internode and a 1 µm node. What percentage of its length is covered by myelin?
cards.back: Covered fraction = 50/(50 + 1) = 50/51 ≈ 0.9804, or about 98%. This idealized geometry does not establish fuel dependence.
cards.quote: A node is about a micrometre long.
cards.section: An axon has a supply problem

cards.front: Glycolysis of one glucose to two pyruvate gives a net yield of {{c1::two ATP}}.
cards.quote: Glycolysis splits one glucose into two pyruvate in the cytosol, with a net gain of two ATP

cards.front: How does reducing pyruvate to lactate allow glycolysis to continue without mitochondrial respiration?
cards.back: Lactate dehydrogenase regenerates cytosolic NAD+, allowing glycolysis to keep running.
cards.quote: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+ in the cytosol.

cards.front: A neuron can import lactate, but conversion of lactate to pyruvate is blocked. What happens to its ability to use that imported carbon as mitochondrial fuel, and why?
cards.back: It cannot use that lactate carbon by the stated route: lactate must first become pyruvate before it can be burned in mitochondria.
cards.quote: A cell that takes up lactate can turn it back into pyruvate and burn it in its own mitochondria.

cards.front: Complete glucose oxidation can yield about 30–32 ATP. If a glial cell stops at two lactates and keeps 2 ATP, what fraction of the potential ATP yield remains in those lactates?
cards.back: At the endpoints: (30 − 2)/30 = 28/30 ≈ 93.3%; (32 − 2)/32 = 30/32 ≈ 93.75%. About 93–94% remains as potential yield.
cards.quote: The two lactates still carry about 28 to 30 of those 30 to 32 ATP, more than nine-tenths.

cards.front: In an astrocyte energy model, clearing each glutamate costs 2 ATP. Assume glycolysis supplies all ATP, giving 2 ATP and 2 lactates per glucose, and all lactate is released. How many lactates accompany clearance of 3,000 glutamates?
cards.back: ATP needed = 3,000 × 2 = 6,000. Glucose used = 6,000/2 = 3,000. Lactate released = 3,000 × 2 = 6,000 molecules.
cards.quote: A cell that stops at lactate keeps 2 ATP and passes on the rest.

cards.front: In PLP-null or CNP-null mice, electron microscopy shows nearly normal-looking myelin, but axons later swell and degenerate. Does this identify fuel loss as the cause?
cards.back: No. It suggests glia provide more than insulation, making fuel a candidate. Normal appearance neither proves normal insulation nor identifies the missing support.
cards.quote: The simplest reading is that the glial cell gives the axon something besides insulation.
cards.section: Myelin that looked fine, axons that did not

cards.front: Which respiratory-chain complex requires Cox10 for its assembly?
cards.back: Complex IV, the last step of the respiratory chain.
cards.quote: Cox10 is needed to assemble complex IV, the last step of the respiratory chain.
cards.section: Switch off the glial cell's respiration

cards.front: What did preserved adult CNS axons and myelin after Cox10 deletion in myelinating cells establish about mature oligodendrocytes?
cards.back: Mature oligodendrocytes can survive on glycolysis, and their respiration was unnecessary for axonal preservation over the months studied. This alone did not demonstrate fuel transfer.
cards.quote: Oligodendrocytes that have made their myelin can live on glycolysis alone, and the axons did not need their oligodendrocytes to respire.
cards.section: Switch off the glial cell's respiration

cards.front: Why should the peripheral neuropathy after Cox10 deletion not be taken as proof of an intrinsic metabolic difference between all Schwann cells and all oligodendrocytes?
cards.back: Schwann cells lost respiration while dividing and myelinating; the spared oligodendrocytes had already made myelin. Developmental stage may explain part of the difference.
cards.quote: Part of the difference may be the stage of myelination, not only the cell type.
cards.section: Switch off the glial cell's respiration

cards.front: In Cox10-mutant brains, suppose lactate production stays high but its consumption slows under anaesthesia. What happens to detectable lactate, and does that locate its normal consumer?
cards.back: Lactate accumulates under anaesthesia and falls when consumption resumes. This fits the observation but does not identify the consumer; axonal uptake was not traced.
cards.quote: In an awake animal, something uses that lactate as fast as it is made; under anaesthesia, that use slows and the excess builds up.
cards.section: Switch off the glial cell's respiration

cards.front: In the reporter-mouse study of glial fuel supply, which cells were enriched in MCT1?
cards.back: Oligodendrocytes.
cards.quote: to show that one of them, MCT1, is concentrated in oligodendrocytes.

cards.front: In a hypothetical neuron–glia culture, blocking a fuel transporter kills neurons during glucose withdrawal. Added lactate restores survival while the blocker remains. What does this rescue support?
cards.back: Loss of an available monocarboxylate fuel likely contributes to neuronal death. Lactate can replace the missing support under these conditions; rescue does not exclude every drug effect.
cards.quote: Because lactate rescued the neurons, the best reading is that they were missing lactate, a monocarboxylate that MCT1 carries and that glia are thought to supply.

cards.front: A slice-wide MCT1 inhibitor causes neuronal loss. How would a genetic comparison better test whether oligodendroglial MCT1 matters, and what would it still leave unresolved?
cards.back: Delete MCT1 only in the oligodendrocyte lineage and compare axonal integrity with controls across age. Cell restriction addresses the drug's cell-target ambiguity, but degeneration still would not trace fuel or establish its direction of transfer.
cards.why: Rule: a perturbation acting on every cell cannot identify which cell's transporter mattered; cell-restricted deletion narrows that attribution.
cards.quote: The drug also acts on every cell in the slice (and inhibitors of this kind can also reach MCT2 in neurons)

cards.front: A mouse lacks MCT1 only in oligodendrocyte-lineage cells and appears normal when young. Based on the lineage-deletion experiment, what should be checked as it ages, and why?
cards.back: Check for axonal degeneration and thinning myelin. These emerged with age in the experiment, showing that a normal young phenotype does not exclude a long-term requirement.
cards.quote: Young mice were normal. Only as the mice aged did axons degenerate, and myelin thinned.

cards.front: How do preserved axons after glial Cox10 deletion and late degeneration after oligodendroglial MCT1 deletion support a fuel-export model, and why is the comparison incomplete?
cards.back: They fit glycolytic glia exporting fuel that axons burn: glial respiration was dispensable over the observed months, whereas oligodendroglial MCT1 mattered with age. The cohorts were not followed over matched ages, and late myelin thinning could contribute to damage.
cards.why: Rules: glycolysis makes lactate or pyruvate available, and axons can burn pyruvate. These complementary perturbations support the model but do not follow carbon between cells.
cards.quote: One caution: the two sets of mice were not followed over matched ages, and MCT1 loss also thinned myelin late.

cards.front: In the oligodendrocyte fuel-support model, {{c1::MCT1}} exports lactate or pyruvate from the glial cell.
cards.quote: Oligodendrocytes take up glucose, run glycolysis, and export lactate or pyruvate through MCT1.

cards.front: Which two major gaps remain in the oligodendrocyte-to-axon fuel-support model?
cards.back: The exact route from glial cytoplasm to axon, and the fraction of axonal ATP supplied through this route in a living animal.
cards.quote: Two things are still unknown: the exact route from glial cytoplasm to axon, and how much of an axon's ATP

cards.front: In the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis, how does synaptic glutamate uptake couple neuronal activity to astrocyte fuel production?
cards.back: Glutamate uptake brings sodium into astrocytes. Pumping it out costs ATP, proposed to drive glycolysis and lactate release for neurons.
cards.quote: Glutamate transporters bring sodium in with each glutamate. The sodium pump has to remove that sodium. The pump's demand for ATP drives glycolysis.

cards.front: In the proposed astrocyte-to-neuron fuel shuttle, what is transferred, and where is it made?
cards.back: Lactate made from astrocyte glucose, supplied to neurons as fuel during synaptic activity.
cards.quote: an active synapse makes its astrocyte burn glucose to lactate, and the lactate goes to the neuron as fuel.

cards.front: Why did the astrocyte-culture response to transported D-aspartate, together with blockade by ouabain, support a transport-and-pump mechanism for increased glycolysis?
cards.back: D-aspartate reproduced the response through the same transporters, arguing against receptor activation; sodium-pump blockade prevented it, supporting an ATP demand from removing imported sodium.
cards.quote: D-aspartate, an analogue taken up by the same transporters, had the same effect, and the authors concluded that receptor activation was not responsible.

cards.front: Why does a lactate concentration gradient between astrocytes and neurons provide only partial evidence for the astrocyte-neuron shuttle?
cards.back: A gradient is consistent with transfer but does not measure net flow or establish how much fuel neurons receive.
cards.quote: A gradient fits transfer but does not by itself measure net flow.

cards.front: How can an astrocyte-to-neuron lactate gradient coexist with stimulated neurons increasing their own glycolysis, without either result settling the shuttle debate?
cards.back: A gradient does not establish net flux, and glucose use by neurons does not exclude some astrocyte lactate use. Supply could vary with activity, region and preparation. Compare transfer under matched conditions rather than assuming one universal fuel source.
cards.why: Rules: neurons can use glucose directly; concentration gradients do not measure net flow. Together these limit what either observation can establish about lactate supply.
cards.quote: The answer may differ between resting and active states, between cortex and other regions, and between preparations.

cards.front: An injured Schwann cell increases glycolysis, but its extra lactate and pyruvate cannot leave the cell. What happens to the proposed fuel-mediated benefit for the cut-off axon, and why?
cards.back: That extra fuel cannot support the axon through export. The proposed benefit requires both release from Schwann cells and use by the injured axon; increased glycolysis alone is insufficient.
cards.why: A Schwann-cell glycolytic shift was reported to slow injured axon degeneration in mouse nerve. That finding does not establish a benefit for every injury or time point.
cards.quote: If the extra lactate or pyruvate leaves the Schwann cell and the injured axon uses it, the shift should help, at least for a while;
cards.section: After injury: when glial metabolism changes

cards.front: In a hypothetical neuron experiment, stimulation raises cytosolic NADH. Blocking lactate entry reduces but does not abolish the rise. Can the remaining signal show that neuronal glycolysis stopped?
cards.back: No. Glycolysis itself makes cytosolic NADH and could account for the remaining rise. The reduced component is consistent with lactate use, but NADH alone cannot separate the sources.
cards.quote: An NADH sensor alone cannot tell the sources apart, since glycolysis and lactate conversion both make NADH.

cards.front: Design a tracer test that distinguishes oligodendrocyte-derived lactate oxidation in an axon from the axon using labelled glucose directly.
cards.back: Give labelled glucose first to a separate glial compartment. Measure labelled lactate released by glia and labelled pyruvate and citric acid cycle products in axons. Control tracer leakage and direct axonal glucose uptake; test whether glial MCT1 loss lowers axonal labelling.
cards.why: Rules: glial glycolysis can produce lactate, axons can turn lactate into pyruvate, and axons also use glucose directly. The controls distinguish these routes.
cards.quote: Measure labelled lactate released by the glia and labelled pyruvate and citric acid cycle products in the axon.

cards.front: A lactate sensor in an axon stays steady after surrounding glia stop exporting lactate. Does that rule out a previous glial contribution? Combine fuel metabolism with the limits of a concentration sensor.
cards.back: No. The axon could compensate with its own glycolysis, maintaining lactate concentration after loss of an external source. A steady concentration therefore does not establish unchanged fuel transfer.
cards.why: Rules: axons have their own glycolysis, and a lactate sensor measures the resulting concentration rather than uniquely identifying the fuel source.
cards.quote: the axon could make up the loss with its own glycolysis, so a steady signal would not rule one out.

cards.front: The transcription factor stabilized at low oxygen that turns on glycolytic genes is {{c1::HIF1-alpha}}.
cards.quote: HIF1-alpha, a transcription factor stabilized at low oxygen, turns on glycolytic genes.
cards.section: What steers the glycolytic shift after injury

cards.front: How does the mouse satellite-glia result after peripheral nerve injury broaden the idea of glial metabolic support beyond fuel?
cards.back: Satellite glia activate fatty acid synthesis, a program reported to help sensory axons regrow. Glial metabolism may support membrane production as well as energy supply.
cards.quote: satellite glia turn on genes for fatty acid synthesis, and that this program helps the sensory axons regrow.
cards.section: Satellite glia and lipids for regrowth

cards.front: In mice whose Schwann cells cannot maintain mitochondrial DNA, abnormal Schwann cells were reported to release acylcarnitines, proposed contributors to axonal damage. Design a comparison that distinguishes a harmful released metabolite from simple loss of fuel support.
cards.back: Compare axons given the same fuel supply with and without the released acylcarnitines. Extra damage with acylcarnitines would support an active toxic contribution rather than fuel withdrawal alone; it would not establish the entire cause of neuropathy in vivo.
cards.why: Rule: glial metabolism can actively release damaging metabolites, as well as fail to supply fuel. Holding fuel availability constant separates these candidate explanations.
cards.quote: the metabolically abnormal Schwann cells release acylcarnitines, lipid metabolites that damage axons, and proposed this as one contributor to the neuropathy.

cards.front: Which brain cells hold most of the brain's glycogen stores?
cards.back: Astrocytes.
cards.quote: glycogen, a stored form of glucose that in the brain is held mostly in astrocytes.

cards.front: A white-matter energy budget assigns a larger share of expenditure to upkeep than signalling. Can that result alone show that glial fuel mainly pays for upkeep?
cards.back: No. A budget partitions demand, not fuel sources. It cannot identify which demands are met by glial supply.
cards.quote: A budget like this does not say which demands glial fuel meets.

cards.front: Which two proposed costs could make increased glial glycolysis harmful after nerve injury, and how certain are they?
cards.back: Proton-associated lactate output could acidify tissue, and a glial repair program could divert resources from axons. Neither cost is established in injured nerve.
cards.quote: Two possible costs of a large glial glycolytic response have been proposed, and neither is established in injured nerve.
